steps.observation: How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Here’s a high-level, conceptual breakdown of how a Transformer works:

1. Input Representation  
  • Tokens (words, subwords) are first mapped to continuous vectors (“embeddings”).  
  • Since there’s no recurrence or convolution to encode order, a fixed or learned positional encoding is added to each embedding so the model knows the word order.

2. Self-Attention Mechanism  
  • For each position in the input sequence, we compute three vectors by multiplying the embedding by three different learned matrices:  
    – Query (Q)  
    – Key (K)  
    – Value (V)  
  • Attention scores are computed by taking the dot product of Q with every K, then scaling and applying softmax to get a weight distribution.  
  • Each position’s output is the weighted sum of all Vs—this lets every token “attend” to (i.e. gather information from) every other token in the sequence.

3. Multi-Head Attention  
  • Instead of doing one big attention, we split Q/K/V into multiple “heads” (subspaces).  
  • Each head learns different patterns of interaction.  
  • Their outputs are concatenated and projected back to the model’s full dimensionality.

4. Position-wise Feed-Forward Network  
  • After attention, each position’s vector passes through the same small feed-forward network (usually two linear layers with a ReLU or GELU in between).  
  • This adds nonlinearity and further transforms the representation.

5. Residual Connections & Layer Normalization  
  • Around both the multi-head attention block and the feed-forward block, residual (skip) connections are added.  
  • Layer normalization is applied to stabilize and speed up training.

6. Stacking Layers  
  • A Transformer encoder stacks N identical layers of (self-attention → feed-forward).  
  • A Transformer decoder does similarly but adds an extra “encoder–decoder attention” step so the decoder can attend to encoder outputs, and it masks future tokens for autoregressive generation.

7. Output & Training  
  • In language tasks, the decoder’s final output vectors go through a linear layer + softmax to predict the next token.  
  • The model is trained end-to-end on large corpora, minimizing cross-entropy loss between predicted and true tokens.

Key conceptual takeaway:  
Transformers replace recurrence with global, parallelizable attention. This lets them model long-range dependencies more directly and efficiently, which is why they excel at translation, summarization, language modeling, and many other sequence tasks.
